newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Sarajevo hopes run high before Papal visit.
newsitem.headline: Sarajevo hopes run high before Papal visit.

text.p: Hopes ran high among Sarajevans on Saturday that Pope John Paul II's visit to the war-scarred city could breathe life into a fragile peace and promote reconciliation over nationalist bigotry.
"I wish the Pope could influence our leaders and change the way they think," said Jusuf Granulo, hours before the Pope was due to arrive.
"He should have come much sooner," said Granulo, a 52-year old lawyer.

In a country bitterly divided by nationalist hatred more than a year after the war ended, Sarajevo is still a rare oasis that harbours Bosnia's three communities -- Moslems, Catholic Croats and Orthodox Christian Serbs -- who defied calls by hardliners for separate communities.
Sarajevans said they believe the Pope's visit carried political symbolism that might help efforts at restoring co-existence.
"Everywhere he went he brought peace. I hope he does the same for us," Hedija, 32, said.
Bosnia's troubled Moslem-Croat federation is in desperate need of a boost after relations deteriorated in February, sparking a series of tit-for-tat bombings of Catholic churches and Islamic mosques.
The Pope snubbed Croat hardline nationalists by declining invitations to visit the western Herzegovina region where they dominate.
The Pope's support for a multi-ethnic Bosnia has made him a favourite with Bosnian Moslem leaders, who have gone out of their way to welcome him to the capital.
Preparations for the Papal visit were in full swing on Saturday morning.
Potholes on streets which might be used by the Pope's motorcade were patched up and lanes freshly painted.
As a security precaution, residents in flats overlooking the Papal route were told by Bosnian police not to approach their windows as the Pontiff passes by.
City cleaners scrubbed Alipasina street which runs up to Kosevo stadium, where the Pope will hold an open-air mass for an estimated 40,000 people on Sunday.
One of the workers enthusiastically washed a row of flower pots lining the street. "The president of all Catholics is coming to our town and we want him to feel good here," Esad Sinanovic, 47, said.
In the same stadium where opening ceremonies were held for the 1984 Olympic games, some 300 workers put final touches on an altar.

The Pope, who often spoke of Sarajevo's wartime suffering, was forced to cancel a planned visit to Sarajevo in 1994 while war was still raging because the Bosnian Serbs beseiging the city said they could not guarantee his safety.
Some Sarajevans said this visit was a bit anti-climatic.
"If he had come the first time he would have been a real hero. Now, I'm not so excited about it," said Azra.
